html:
The mosque Suleiman the Magnificent built on the third hill of Istanbul in memory of his son Şehzade Mehmed, the eldest son of Hurrem Sultan, who died in 1543 on his way home from a campaign in Hungary. Mehmed's tomb was finished in 1544, and the mosque and its complex were built from 1545 to 1548. It was the first great imperial commission of Mimar Sinan.

The plan is a square under a central dome 19 m wide and 37 m high, with a half dome on each of the four sides and small domes in the corners: a fully symmetrical layout that earlier Ottoman builders had worked toward. Sinan gathered the weight onto four pillars and a few buttresses, which let him open the walls with more windows, and hid the buttresses outside behind domed porches along the sides. The twin minarets, each with two balconies, carry carved geometric relief unusual on Ottoman minarets. A forecourt as large as the mosque has arches of pink and white stone.

Sinan called it his apprentice work and never repeated the plan, moving on to the single great domes of the Süleymaniye and the Selimiye. Later architects copied it, in the Blue Mosque, the New Mosque and the rebuilt Fatih Mosque. In the garden behind stand Mehmed's octagonal tomb, lined with coloured tiles and with a wooden throne over his coffin to mark him as heir, and the tomb of the grand vizier Rüstem Pasha, covered in Iznik tiles.
